text: You've right-sized CPU VMs throughout this path by picking the smallest instance that comfortably handles peak load. GPU right-sizing starts from the same instinct, but it splits into two real problems the moment you separate training from inference, because those two jobs put very different demands on the hardware.

Training has to hold several things in GPU memory at once: the model's parameters, the optimizer state - which for Adam can be two to three times the parameter count on its own - the activations retained from the forward pass so backpropagation can use them, and the gradients. Inference only needs the parameters and the activations for whatever request is currently in flight. No optimizer state, no stored gradients, no backward pass at all.

That gap is exactly why training a large model often needs a GPU with very large memory, or several GPUs working together through the data- and model-parallelism techniques from earlier in this path. A model that fits comfortably on one mid-tier GPU for inference can easily need several times that memory just to train - the extra cost isn't the model, it's everything training has to keep around that inference never touches.

Because of that gap, inference can frequently run on a smaller, cheaper GPU than the one used to train the same model - and for genuinely small models, sometimes on CPU with no GPU at all. The right question for inference isn't what hardware trained the model, it's what's the smallest compute that meets this model's real latency and throughput needs under actual traffic, tested on its own.

The practical discipline is the same habit as right-sizing a CPU VM, applied to GPU metrics: track memory and compute utilization across a real training run, and load-test the actual serving endpoint before assuming it needs a bigger GPU. Defaulting to the biggest GPU available because it's simpler to provision is exactly the instinct that drives runaway spend. Next lesson turns all of this into a concrete FinOps practice for AI infrastructure.
